pages.seoTitle: Bhansa Nepal: hot school lunches for children in Sindhupalchok
pages.seoDescription: We cook dal bhat and a seasonal vegetable in four school kitchens in Melamchi, every school day. Rs 45 pays for one child’s lunch. See where the money goes.

props.title: A hot lunch at school, every school day
props.text: In four hill schools in Melamchi, Sindhupalchok, village cooks serve rice, dal and a seasonal vegetable at half past eleven. Children stay for afternoon class, and more of them come back the next morning.

image.alt: Children in blue school uniforms at their desks, one of them smiling at the camera

props.eyebrow: Rs 45 pays for one child’s lunch · Four schools, about 600 children

items.text: Rice, dal and tarkari
An egg on Fridays

Served at 11:30 sharp

props.quote: The head teacher in Talamarang asked us why his afternoon class was always half empty. The answer was lunch. We started with one pot and his school kitchen in Shrawan 2076.
props.name: Sabina Tamang

props.heading: What one plate of dal bhat does

image.alt: Two women sifting rice and cooking over a wood fire in a school kitchen

items.title: It pays two village mothers a fair wage
items.text: Each school kitchen is run by two cooks chosen by the parents’ committee. They are paid the national minimum wage, on time, into their own bank account, and they know every child by name.

image.alt: Women selling vegetables and marigolds from baskets at a village market

items.title: It buys from farms the children walk past
items.text: Rice and dal come from the Melamchi bazaar; greens, pumpkin, radish and potatoes come from farmers within an hour’s walk. Most of the money stays in the ward.

image.alt: Two schoolgirls in blue uniforms smiling in their classroom

items.title: It keeps children in class after noon
items.text: Before lunch started, head teachers told us that many older children left at the break to eat at home, often an hour’s climb away. Most now stay until four.

props.heading: A school day, from the kitchen
props.intro: The same rhythm in all four schools, six days a week.

image.alt: A cook stirring a big pot of vegetable curry over a wood fire

items.title: The vegetables arrive
items.text: A farmer or the cooks themselves bring what is ready that week. The cooks weigh it and write it in the kitchen book.

items.title: Rice washed, fire lit
items.text: Forty kilos of rice for the biggest school. Dal soaks from the night before. The fire is lit from wood the school collects.

items.title: Lunch, class by class
items.text: The youngest eat first. Children wash their hands at the tap, bring their own plate, and sit in rows on the veranda.

items.title: Pots washed, register signed
items.text: A teacher counts the plates served and signs the book. We check the count against attendance every month.

props.heading: What your gift pays for
props.intro: Every rupee below is spent in the schools. Office costs are covered separately by two family foundations.

props.heading: The four schools
props.intro: All in Melamchi Municipality, between 45 minutes and two hours’ walk from the road.

items.title: Talamarang
items.text: Our first kitchen, since Shrawan 2076. Grades 1 to 8, and a new tin roof over the veranda where children eat.

items.title: Bhotang
items.text: The highest school, at 1,900 metres. Lunch here includes a glass of hot milk tea in Poush and Magh.

items.title: Chanaute
items.text: Joined in 2079 after the parents’ committee raised half the cost of a new kitchen.

items.title: Sipa Ghat
items.text: Next to the river. The school garden grows most of the greens from Kartik to Falgun.

props.heading: How a school joins
props.intro: We add one school a year, when the money for three years of lunches is already in the bank.

items.title: The school asks
items.text: A head teacher or parents’ committee writes to us. We never approach a school first.

items.title: We visit and count
items.text: Two days at the school: attendance, the kitchen, the water, the road for deliveries.

items.title: Parents choose the cooks
items.text: At an open meeting, with the ward chair present.

items.title: The first lunch
items.text: Usually at the start of a new term, with everyone’s families invited.

items.q: Does the government not already give school meals?
items.a: The government’s day-meal programme covers the youngest grades in public schools. We work alongside it: we top up its budget so the plate includes vegetables and an egg, and we cover the older grades it does not reach.
Yes, by bank transfer to our account in Nepal. We send a receipt in Nepali and English within a week.

items.q: Will I know which child I am feeding?
items.a: If the parents agree, we send the first name and class of one child and a photo from the school each term. We never share surnames or where a family lives.

items.q: How do I know the money arrives?
items.a: Our accounts are audited every year by a chartered accountant and published on this site. Every school kitchen keeps a book of plates served, signed daily by a teacher.

props.title: Rs 1,080 feeds one child for a month
props.text: Give once, or every month. You will hear from the school at the end of each term.

pages.title: How it works
pages.seoTitle: How our school lunches work: kitchens, cooks and the weekly menu
pages.seoDescription: Two cooks per school, vegetables from nearby farms, a menu that changes with the season and a register signed every day. How Bhansa Nepal runs four school kitchens.

props.title: Four kitchens, eight cooks and one register signed every day
props.text: Everything we do happens in the school, run by people from the village. Our field officer visits each kitchen every week.

image.alt: A hill school’s buildings and dirt courtyard in low evening sun

props.heading: Why a cooked lunch, not a biscuit packet
props.body:
Packaged snacks are easier to hand out, but they fill a child for an hour and leave the wrapper in the stream. A plate of rice, dal and vegetables keeps a ten-year-old going until four, costs about the same, and puts wages and vegetable money into the village.

It is also what children eat at home. Nobody has to learn to like it.

props.heading: This month’s menu
props.intro: Mangsir. Greens change with what the farmers bring; the cooks decide on the day.

items.title: Sunday
items.text: Rice, masoor dal, potato and cauliflower tarkari.

items.title: Monday
items.text: Rice, black dal, rayo saag, radish achar.

items.title: Tuesday
items.text: Rice, mixed dal, pumpkin and chickpea tarkari.

items.title: Wednesday
items.text: Beaten rice with soybeans and a bowl of seasonal vegetable soup.

items.title: Thursday
items.text: Rice, mung dal, mustard greens and potato.

items.title: Friday
items.text: Rice, dal, egg curry, and tomato achar. A banana for anyone who does not eat eggs.

image.alt: Schoolchildren looking at a nutrition corner display with signs in Nepali

props.heading: The nutrition corner
props.body:
Each school has a wall where children weigh and measure themselves at the start of every term, with the school nurse or a health volunteer. It is how we know whether lunch is working.

Grade 7 draws the posters. This year’s theme was eggs.

items.title: One pot in Talamarang
items.text: Lunch for 140 children, cooked on a borrowed stove.

items.title: Kept open through the lockdown
items.text: When schools closed, the cooks packed dry rations for families to collect every fortnight.

items.title: Bhotang joins
items.text: The highest school, and the first with a new smokeless stove.

items.title: Chanaute joins

items.title: Sipa Ghat joins

items.title: Eggs every Friday
items.text: Paid for by a monthly giving group of 48 people.

props.heading: Where the schools are
props.note: About three hours by road from Kathmandu. Visits are arranged through our office and always with the head teacher’s agreement.

props.heading: How you can check
props.body:
We are registered with the District Administration Office, Lalitpur, and affiliated with the Social Welfare Council. Our office rent, the founder’s salary and the audit are paid by two family foundations, so they do not come out of your gift.

  • Every kitchen keeps a daily book of plates served, signed by a teacher.
  • Vegetable purchases are recorded with the farmer’s name and the weight.
  • The full audited accounts and the auditor’s letter are sent to anyone who asks, within a week.

If anything in our accounts looks wrong to you, write to the board chair directly at board@bhansanepal.org.np.

props.heading: The people responsible
props.intro: The board meets every two months. Board members are not paid.

people.name: Sabina Tamang
people.bio: Grew up in Helambu. Taught primary school for nine years.

people.name: Nirmala Shrestha
people.bio: Accountant. Checks every month’s spending against the kitchen books.

people.name: Kamal Lama
people.bio: Lives in Melamchi and visits each school every week.

items.q: Why not say how many meals you have served?
items.a: We do, in the annual report, counted from the kitchen books. We would rather send you the book totals than put a round number on the home page.

items.q: Do you take money from companies?
items.a: Yes, for lunches only, and never in exchange for logos in schools or on children’s plates.

items.q: What happens to money given for a school that closes?
items.a: It goes to the other kitchens, and we tell you.

props.title: Want the full accounts?
props.text: Ask and we will email the audited report and the auditor’s letter within a week.

pages.title: Give or volunteer
pages.seoTitle: Give school lunches or volunteer a kitchen day in Melamchi
pages.seoDescription: Give by bank transfer, mobile wallet or at our Kupondole office. Pledge a month of lunches, ask for the accounts, or join a kitchen day in Sindhupalchok.

props.title: Give lunch, once or every month
props.text: Rs 1,080 feeds one child for a month. Tell us below how you would like to give and we will send the details, or come to the office for a cup of tea.

image.alt: Children in blue uniforms eating their midday meal sitting on the floor

props.eyebrow: Receipts in Nepali and English within a week

items.title: Bank transfer
items.text: To our account at a commercial bank in Kupondole. We send the account details by email when you pledge, so you can check them with us first.

items.title: Mobile wallet
items.text: Scan the QR code at our office or on the letter we send you. Good for monthly giving from Rs 1,080.

items.title: At the office
items.text: Cash or cheque at Kupondole Height, Sunday to Friday. You get a receipt on the spot.

props.heading: Pledge, or ask us anything
props.text: Say how much and how often, or ask for the audited accounts. Sabina or Nirmala will reply within two working days.
props.success: Thank you. We will reply within two working days with the details.

image.alt: A woman washing large cooking pots in a school yard

props.heading: Spend a day in a school kitchen
props.body:
Twice a term we take up to six visitors to Melamchi for a kitchen day: vegetables at seven, serving at half past eleven, washing up, and tea with the cooks.

The visit costs Rs 3,500 for the jeep and a meal. It is not a photo trip; we ask visitors to leave cameras in the bag while children eat.

props.heading: Join a kitchen day
props.text: Pick a school and a date that suits you. We confirm by phone once the head teacher agrees.
props.services:
Talamarang (easy road)
Chanaute (45 minute walk)
Sipa Ghat (by the river)
Whichever school needs hands
props.success: Thank you. We will call you within a week to confirm the date.

props.heading: A letter from the schools each term
props.text: Three emails a year, with the kitchen book totals and a photo from each school.
props.success: Thank you. The next letter goes out at the end of term.
